title: Forgive us
hookLine: a gentle tap on the chest as forgiveness is asked
carry: easier when you don't let it build up
last: THE WAY BACK WAS ALREADY BUILT IN.

lines: A HAND COMES UP TO THE CHEST.
TWO LIGHT TAPS OVER THE HEART.
cards: Three times a day, on weekdays, in the middle of a silent prayer, people's right hands come up and touch their chests. Not a punch. Not a dramatic gesture.
Two light taps with a loose fist, over the heart, so small you'd miss them from across the room. Then the hand goes down, and the prayer goes on.
It happens on two words, two words people find hard to say, even in a whisper.

teach.h: WE HAVE SINNED. WE HAVE TRANSGRESSED.
teach.b: The sixth blessing says: forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned. Pardon us, our King, for we have transgressed. For You pardon and forgive.
Blessed are You, gracious One, who forgives abundantly. The two words are chatanu, we have sinned, and pashanu, we have transgressed. At each one, many people tap their chest.
The custom is often explained this way: the heart is where wanting starts, so that's where you knock. And it's we, not I. Even alone, you pray in the plural.
The word for forgiveness here is selichah. Some readers note that in the Hebrew Bible, the verb behind it, salach, is used of God doing the forgiving.
When Moses pleads for the people after the spies, God answers, in the old Jewish translation: "I have pardoned according to thy word." Jews hear that line again every year on the night of Yom Kippur.

The blessing's ending, who forgives abundantly, echoes Isaiah: let the wicked return to God, "for He will abundantly pardon." The Talmud's order makes sense now: understanding, then return, then forgiveness.
You see what you did, you turn around, and then you ask to be let go of it. And it's said every weekday, not once a year. Forgiveness in the Amidah isn't a dramatic event.
It's maintenance, like brushing your teeth: small, daily, and much easier when you don't let it build up.

how: Selach lanu is the sixth blessing of the weekday Amidah; many Jews lightly strike the left side of the chest with the right fist at the words chatanu and pashanu.

games.q: you reach the words we have sinned in the silent Amidah. what do many people do?
o: bow all the way to the floor.
tap the chest lightly, over the heart.

games.why: a light tap over the heart at chatanu and pashanu: small, daily, and easy to miss.

practice: Go back over the last day or two and find one real, recent thing you wish you hadn't done, not the worst thing in your life: a sharp word, a corner cut, a person ignored.
Name it to yourself honestly, and if you like, tap your chest once, gently. If you pray, you can ask to be forgiven; then let your hand rest.
